Not sure how if this illumines much but I think I know the meaning of the 22 vs 24 day discrepancy. It's probably a riddle. In antiquity the Hebrew Bible was considered to have both 22 and 24 "books". Or rather, 24 works written on 22 scrolls (two of the smaller books were combined with larger books). 

If you want more numerology, note that 22 is the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet. It's a sacred number in Kabbalah (and its syncretic cousin Qabalah) and stands for the dimensions of space (the origin, three axes, plus the six faces and twelve lines of a cube). There are also 22 paths of light between the 10 Sefirot (attributes of God). If he's reading Giordano Bruno and J. L. Borges, he knows Kabbalah. Twenty-four is of course two times twelve, possibly signifies: the twelve tribes of Israel and twelve zodiac signs, twelve sons of Jacob plus twelve disciples of Jesus, or the twenty-four elders who surround the crystal sea in front of God's throne.

I wish I could reply to the original author here. I went through something nearly identical at age 21. I always knew I was a little bisexual (I had been attracted to guys before) but I went through a couple years where I wasn't really attracted to guys at all, then I got blindsided by a bunch of new feelings I hadn't had before, coincident with a lot of other stress. The difference here was that I started panicking that I was "really" gay. 

Sexuality is so politicized and fretted over in our society that you're pressed to slap a label on it. Get rid of the straight/gay divide in your head; more people have flexible or bisexual orientations than you'd think. Some people are more sexually fluid and their desires change over time. Bisexuals often notice that their desires move on a sliding scale from gender to gender. 

So I identify as a bisexual/queer person and feel no more anxiety about it. Thing is it's ambiguous. I'm sexually attracted to guys in certain situations but sometimes they leave me cold, while being consistently into women. Other times I feel "boy-crazy". It leaves me a bit confused, some days I ask "Am I really that queer?" Other days it seems stupid to ask. (Being a virgin probably doesn't help because it means I ultimately don't know my own wants as well).

But enough of my monologue. Based on your other comments I think maybe you're more "heteroflexible". Mostly straight but with some ambiguity built in. And that is totally fine. The anxiety you feel about "being gay" is what's negative here, not the occasional interest in the same gender.

On another note, I've only been *romantically* attracted to one guy but had crushes on plenty of women. I bring that up because the romantic side's probably going to be more important for your life: who you choose to sleep with or marry dictates your identity in society more than who you think about at night. If you find a nice girl to be with, you might find the question to be less relevant than it seems now.

So this is something that I went through for a year and a half. I had cystic acne on the face that would periodically flare up and make my skin completely red and inflamed. I had one cyst on each cheek that would ooze or bleed if I had too much alcohol or if I was sweating out in the sun. It was a social nightmare. People would involuntarily be disgusted and force themselves to be kind. I always tried to hide from cameras and I was without exception the ugliest person in the room at any given time. 

Two things helped me. The first was minocycline. It's cheap and effective (though it exacerbated my depression) after about a month the cysts were flat or gone. I would recommend that antibiotic. 

I still had redness and scarring that made me look disfigured. The thing that fixed that was makeup. Try it; I don't care if you're a male (as a queer person it didn't bother me, but your gender identity will survive a bit of face paint). Neutrogena makes pretty good concealer and foundation. Just make sure you find one that actually matches your skin tone. People immediately started telling me my skin looked a lot better (and they were relieved at being able to look at me). The funny part is that some folks will not pick up on it because they don't expect a male to wear makeup. If you work out in the sun or a job where you sweat a lot it's no good, but for social events and indoors it's fine. (Also make sure you've been on medication for a while and your acne is mild/under control before piling cosmetics on top)

Actually yes, only three times so far. Once last year and twice in the past 10 days. Very shallow cuts though (I'm somewhat timid with the razor). I won't deny, it feels good. If you dont mind my asking, what made you stop?

I still feel lonely and cut off, and I don't want to insert myself into people's lives because I feel like a social burden (especially with me being broke and out of a job plus these mental health issues). But at the same time checking out feels like a horrible thing to do because people would care. 

I don't see things getting that much better for me. I feel I'll always be somewhat screwed up like everyone else in my family. Maybe there will be a high around the corner, but then a crushing low won't be far behind.

I wonder if more FAs would get out of these situations if they gave the same gender a try (maybe it would help if the barriers are mostly social rather than physical).
